players.product: CPO / silicon-photonics wafer test - insertion-1 known-good-die probe on PIC wafers, plus engineering probers

quarterly_data.signal: CPO REVENUE RAISED AGAIN AND THE CUSTOMER BASE IS BROADENING. CEO Mike Slessor: 'we started the year with a view of maybe $10 million-$20 million in revenue. Have now successfully upgraded that to reaching $20 million by the end of the current third quarter' — i.e. the top of the original full-year range is now hit by the end of Q3. More important than the dollars, the concentration is changing: 'one of the exciting things that we're now seeing in the second part of the year is broader production adoption of this TRITON high-volume manufacturing platform at multiple foundries with multiple fabless customers'. Today it is 'pretty concentrated, with one major foundry fabless partnership', but FormFactor is 'building backlog and building the breadth of the backlog where this diversifies a little bit beyond that one customer set'. Installed base: 'hundreds of systems installed worldwide' at close to as many customers, with 'installed now tens of systems' specifically ramping in CPO production. The 2025 acquisition of Keystone Photonics is described as 'really an enabling technology for optical probing'. On the NPO-versus-CPO debate, Slessor said FormFactor has built one fundamental optical probing technology applicable across CPO, NPO and pluggables, and that NPO is not yet pulling in at the scale CPO is affecting 2026 revenue, though there is 'lots of activity' across the customer base. He also embraced the bottleneck label: photonics test is where the industry is constrained, and FormFactor is resolving technical and operational challenges in real time on installed systems.
quarterly_data.figure: CPO revenue view upgraded from $10 million-$20 million for the year to reaching $20 million by the end of the current third quarter; hundreds of systems installed worldwide; tens of systems in CPO production

quarterly_data.signal: GPU PROBE-CARD MARKET SIZED AND A SHARE TARGET PUT ON IT FOR THE FIRST TIME. Slessor on qualifying for GPU applications at the world's largest foundry: 'we've now received qualification and are shipping pilot production volumes that are being used in production, for GPU test at the world-leading foundry'. On the size: 'We initially sized it maybe a little less than $100 million a year. That feels awfully conservative at this point.' On share against the entrenched incumbent, assuming the uptime/MTBF/test-cell-productivity advantages of FormFactor's advanced MEMS probes hold through the initial production ramp: 'we will be able to gain on the next generation, maybe somewhere in the 20%-25%-30% share range', which he called a useful goal — revenue from it becoming visible in 2027. Delivering it depends on capacity: 'We are pretty constrained on capacity right now.'
quarterly_data.figure: GPU probe-card market initially sized a little less than $100 million a year (now seen as conservative); target 20%-25%-30% share range on the next generation

quarterly_data.signal: CUSTOM ASICs CROSS INTO ADVANCED MEMS IN 2027-2028 — THE NEXT TECHNOLOGY PIVOT. Slessor named the category directly: 'custom ASICs, things like Google's TPU, AWS's Trainium'. Their power envelope, both consumed and produced, is driving them out of legacy wire-based needle probe technology: 'We see custom ASICs really crossing this brink in 2027 and into 2028 of needing an advanced MEMS probe technology... much the same way GPUs did a few generations ago.' It will be mixed rather than wholesale — chiplet architectures mean some chiplets stay on legacy wire probes while the advanced compute chiplets require MEMS. FormFactor builds every probe with proprietary MEMS metallurgy and patterning, vertically integrated in Livermore, California and the ramping Farmers Branch, Texas site, enabling higher current, higher speed and higher/lower temperature test. Engagement is with 'all the names you'd expect us to be engaged with and their foundry and OSAT partners'; initial revenue has been booked on some projects, with designs and qualifications won in late 2026 and ramp in 2027. These may not appear as 10% customers because FormFactor is 'essentially operating at a billion-dollar annual run rate now', raising the 10%-customer bar.
quarterly_data.figure: custom ASICs crossing to advanced MEMS probe in 2027 and into 2028; FormFactor at a billion-dollar annual run rate

quarterly_data.signal: THREE NEW COMPUTE PROBE-CARD WINS DISCLOSED, ALL UNNAMED. (1) 'One of our historic long-term customers, one of the major CPU suppliers to the industry, their business obviously getting stronger associated with some of the turnaround they've done and the CPU strength.' (2) 'We recently qualified and won some designs at a fabless CPU and GPU manufacturer.' (3) 'There's a third customer building their own CPUs for their overall high-performance compute products, where we've won some designs and expect to have that as a 2027 contributor.' Slessor also explained why probe cards stay consumable even though high-performance-compute probes no longer wear out: each new mask set needs a new probe card — 'as a customer like NVIDIA goes from Blackwell to Rubin to Rubin Ultra, those are each new probe cards, even though they use the same capital equipment and test equipment' — so design-change velocity, not wear, now drives the recurring revenue.

CAPACITY IS THE BINDING CONSTRAINT AND FARMERS BRANCH IS THE RELEASE VALVE. Slessor: 'right now, the simplest way to think about our situation is we are capacity constrained. What's limiting our growth, if you will, or what's constraining our growth, is our capacity.' Farmers Branch, Texas is 'close to a 300,000 square foot site' bought a little over a year ago with a ready-to-go clean room and expansion potential; a grand opening is set for 'late October'; the site is expected to deliver 'twice the current California probe card capacity in the current phase'. Timing: 'Start to ship the initial qualification units in the fourth quarter, and again, ramping through 2027 to deliver a substantial increase, essentially 2X the existing capacity as we get through the back part of 2027.' Capacity will be turned on in tranches matched to demand to avoid utilisation and gross-margin headwinds. On the target model — '55% gross margin, $5 of earnings per share on $1.6 billion of revenue' in 2030 — he said the external high-single-digit market growth assumption was arguably too conservative and that FormFactor could 'reach the target model faster than 2030' if demand holds.
quarterly_data.figure: Farmers Branch: close to a 300,000 square foot site, grand opening in late October, twice the current California probe card capacity in the current phase; initial qualification units ship in the fourth quarter, 2X the existing capacity by the back part of 2027; target model 55% gross margin, $5 of earnings per share on $1.6 billion of revenue

players.product: probe cards for HBM/DRAM wafer test

quarterly_data.signal: HBM GROWTH DECOMPOSED, AND THE THIRD DRAM CUSTOMER OPENS UP. On the roughly '70% growth on a year-over-year basis' in HBM in the first half, Slessor attributed it to three things: share gains from 'adding a second HBM customer'; industry bit growth as HBM3 moved to HBM4; and ASP uplift that came not from price increases but from delivering a higher-value configuration 'able to test at the 11 gigabit per second spec of HBM4 and test hundreds of die at once'. FormFactor's largest customer is the HBM leader, where it is the strong incumbent. At the third DRAM maker the major competitor is the entrenched incumbent and FormFactor sees less adoption of its high-speed stack-die configuration — but 'there is a very active conversation with that customer about what to plan for in 2027 and into 2028, as we have more capacity available to serve them'. On the HBM de-spec debate, Slessor called it 'much ado about nothing': fewer/simpler stacks would be offset by more HBM units and by more networking infrastructure to transact data across those units, leaving it 'net net... neutral'. He framed the whole test tailwind as a chiplet problem — in an HBM stack 'one of the 16 die actually causes the entire stack to be essentially scrapped and lost' without known-good-die certainty.
quarterly_data.figure: HBM revenue up about 70% year-over-year in the first half; test at the 11 gigabit per second spec of HBM4 and hundreds of die at once

quarterly_data.signal: DRAM MIX AND WHY PROBE-CARD INTENSITY IS ABOUT TO LOOK BROKEN. Slessor: 'As we go from Q2 to Q3, we expect to again have record levels of DRAM probe card revenue with actually the mix shifting to DDR5 as our customers optimize their wafer start mix and take advantage of very strong spot market pricing' — with gross margin guided 'Up to 54%' including some one-time tariff benefits, against the 55% target model. On intensity: probe card spend as a fraction of customer revenue has run 'around the 0.4% level', but 'we see that distorting pretty substantially' through 2026 into 2027, because per-unit probe card spending is rising far slower than DRAM ASPs, which 'have exploded' on shortage pricing. FormFactor is explicitly not a supply/demand pricer — 'We're a value-based pricer' — so the gross-margin improvement to date and going forward is COGS-focused (yields, cycle times) rather than price-driven.
quarterly_data.figure: record levels of DRAM probe card revenue Q2 to Q3 with mix shifting to DDR5; gross margin guided up to 54%; probe card intensity around the 0.4% level and distorting through 2026 into 2027
